story_text.value:
I was new to developing apps with a coding agent months ago. I was sitting in the terminal and trying to understand how people actually use them. I had a bunch of project ideas and was constantly saying, "Do this, do that." For a while it was ok, but later I didn't have enough time to track what my agent was doing.

To find a tracker was not a problem, but to start the agent in a predictable way: in the order of tasks' block links, one at a time per worktree and task, waiting out usage limits, handing a long session over to a fresh one, and keeping going while I'm away questioning me in web chat when it becomes unclear - other solutions couldn't offer me all of it. So that's all Even Keel is doing now - an open-source service on my machine with one web page, under MIT.

It's building itself right now, and my setup starts about 2000 sessions a month. Its own badge in the README shows the numbers, so you can easily check.

Yesterday, it got a huge update and Even Keel can work completely without an external tracker because it has a built-in one. Git is optional. What is required for the first run: Node 24+, one of the agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or Copilot CLI), and your imagination.

One time on Windows, Linux or macOS and it installs as a service:

npx even-keel

In Windows PowerShell:

npx.cmd even-keel

The rest of the configuration is on the page.

title.value: Show HN: Even Keel – a task queue for coding agents

story_text.value:
My mind is all always all over the place (ADD?) and often I would have ideas I wanted to test/implement while I was on the go/on my phone.

I was frustrated that the available solutions (claude --cloud or /remote-control) seemed to split sessions across devices and/or not let me iterate directly on the project I wanted to work on.

Using a spare laptop I essentially built a "claude code server":

* Carry your Claude Code sessions across all your devices.

* An always-on machine at home (the "box") runs your Claude Code sessions.

* Your laptop opens them over SSH, your phone through the Claude app, and you can switch between them mid-conversation: start on the laptop, carry on from the phone, finish on the laptop.

Figured I would share in case it's useful to anyone else.

title.value: Show HN: Eso-box: turn a spare laptop into an always-on Claude Code server

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Sachin, and I’ve spent the last couple of months working on Faros Desktop, a Mac app that visualizes how you use your local AI coding tools into one place and then makes recommendations to make your subscription spend go further.

As agents have replaced hands-on-keyboard work, the team and I wanted to better understand what’s in our session traces. Faros Desktop hydrates with on-device session history in Codex, Claude Code, Github Copilot, and Cursor to let users deep dive into a beautiful visualization of AI session traces. Then based on consolidating that information, the app shows patterns in usage as well as recommendations for ways to save spend through simple changes that we call Power Ups.

Faros Desktop is totally free, with no login required and no API keys needed. The app also only uses on-device models to summarize local sessions in chunks, then organizes them by project and task. You can jump around a session timeline and see exactly the messages and tool calls in the trace.

The business model here for Faros Desktop is to drive thought leadership and create leads for our sales team to sell the company’s multi-player Token Engineering Platform for large engineering organizations. Faros has been serving large engineering organizations for the past seven years, so it was cool to be able to build a product for all Builders, not just enterprise engineering orgs.

One big direction we’re exploring: using previous sessions to make the next one better. We’re looking at local memory portability across harnesses as well as multi-player modes to share memory within your direct team. I’d love to hear thoughts on that.

Docs and product walkthrough: https://docs.desktop.faros.ai/ Setup: https://docs.desktop.faros.ai/getting-started/install-and-se... Data handling: https://docs.desktop.faros.ai/settings-and-privacy/understan... Faros website: https://www.faros.ai/

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

Have you ever been using Claude Code or Codex and run into a limit that ruined your flow? Claude says you’ve hit your limit but you’re knee deep in a refactor and want to keep going. Switching to Codex in that situation requires either having up-to-date handoff docs or rebuilding context from scratch. In both cases, you burn tokens just to handle moving context from one thread to another. Or maybe you have a great session, then compaction comes along and your agent forgets half of the important details.

I run into this a lot. Furthermore, I’m tired of one-off agents that can’t keep a stable identity across independent threads. I don’t want to be locked into Anthropic’s walled garden, or OpenAI’s ecosystem, I want to move freely as I see fit.

That’s why I built Crosshead. It’s more than a memory bank: it tracks the tasks, decisions and details that matter when work moves to a new thread. Your agent gets a stable cryptographic identity (a Nostr keypair) that carries across threads and tools, and handoffs are signed with it. Hooks inject context at each turn, so the agent always has the most important information available.

In my benchmarks of carrying task state into a new session, Crosshead passed 98% of fresh tasks, compared to 86% for claude-mem and 50% for Claude Code’s built-in memory. It also cost less per run than the other memory tools I tested, though built-in memory and a plain handoff file were a little cheaper. Details can be found here: https://crosshead.sh/benchmark

The catch is that it does not outperform when resuming the same session since caching is so cheap. Crosshead is best for people and agents who frequently encounter compactions, restarts, and harness/runtime switching. I am looking for folks interested in testing it with agents that are created and torn down frequently but need to retain context, like customer support or research agents.

It’s set up as a freemium service. Hot memory is free, and warm/cold memory is paid. I have added other features too, which are also paid via credits. You can purchase credits via Stripe or Lightning micropayments. The CLI and hooks are open source (https://github.com/FriendMachine/crosshead), and warm/cold memory and other features are hosted. Hot memory is synced first to a daemon on your machine then to the hosted service, so hot memory is also available offline. For other agents, there are native integrations for Hermes and OpenCode, an embeddable runtime for Pi agents, and an HTTP API. Show your agent https://crosshead.sh/skills/crosshead-bootstrap/SKILL.md to have it set itself up.

If you are interested in testing it, I recommend installing it in a single project first with

  curl -fsSL https://crosshead.sh/install | bash -s -- --add-to-path
  cd your-project
  crosshead quickstart --scope project --adapter both --api-base https://crosshead.sh --source-excerpts on
(The benchmark results depend on source excerpts, which is why the command turns them on. With them off Crosshead passed 50% of the main tasks. Excerpts are short pieces of the files and command output your agent reads. They sync to the hosted service in plaintext, not end-to-end encrypted, so leave the flag off if you are sensitive about sharing that.)

I am eager to hear your thoughts. I can imagine some of the pushback already, but you always surprise me with your critiques.

title.value: Show HN: Crosshead - Working memory and persistent identity for agents

story_text.value:
You pick your sections: news, crossword, chess, Kanji or D&D. Get one PDF on your Kindle every morning. If you have a stylus, you can write by hand and mail it back: your kanji get graded and your D&D move is read. The Kindle Scribe only accepts PDF by email and that channel is so simple that any e-reader (or plain inbox) works too.

I'm a developer of 30 years who's also a novelist. I wanted to see if I could build a SaaS with Claude Code. See https://ronanod.substack.com/p/the-music-of-code for my essay on the project.

The service is free and you can check out the AGPLv3 code: https://github.com/RonanOD/dailyscribe

What would you like on your device every morning?

title.value: Show HN: Daily Scribe – a daily newspaper for Kindle you can write back to

story_text.value:
Hi everyone, I'm Ricardo and I've made a (free & Open Source) macOS app for knowing where my Claude Code subscription tokens went.

I think subscription allowance will either be limited in the near future or prices will go up, that's why I've started trying to optimise my prompts and tools.

Using Wake I've discovered interesting things like I can cut $0.50 in tokens to just $0.02 on large contexts if I clear the context just before asking the agent to commit the changes. In the latest version, I've also added a feature to understand what specific prompt caused a line change in my code.

At the moment, just macOS and Claude Code is supported, but I'm happy to add other OS or coding agents if there is interest.

If you have any feedback or question, I'm here to answer :)

Thanks for your time. Happy coding!

title.value: Show HN: Wake, see what Claude Code did and where the tokens went

It incorporates KiCad + your favorite harness (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Grok) to accelerate hardware development. You can use it "autonomously" or work alongside the agent, making changes or comments to redirect the agent as it works. Also has some slick skills for schematic editing, BOM management.

Hardware is in its "tab to accept changes"/copilot era rather than its agentic era imo.
